sets.title: Fireflies and the last train

sets.title: Counting bees in the clover
sets.transcript:
M: Come in. You wanted to talk about your project proposal? I read it last night.
W: Yes. Is it all right? I want to count the bees that visit the clover behind the gym.
M: It's a nice idea, and the clover's full of flowers right now, but I'm worried about the timing. Projects are due in the second week of October, and by then it'll be getting cold.
W: Bees still come out on warm afternoons in October, though, don't they?
M: Some do. But a few years ago a student of mine tried something similar with butterflies. We had two weeks of rain, and he ended up with almost nothing to write about. He had to start again with a library project.
W: I thought about that, actually. That's why I've started already, instead of waiting until October. I've done three counts this week.
M: Three already? When did you find the time for that?
W: At lunch on Monday, Wednesday and today. Ten minutes each time, in the same spot. I counted fourteen bees on Monday and almost thirty today.
M: Thirty. Was it warmer today?
W: Much warmer. On Monday it was cloudy and a bit windy, and today it was really sunny. So I'd like to write down the temperature each time too, from the thermometer outside the science room.
M: Hmm. That actually makes it a stronger project. You wouldn't just be counting bees. You'd be asking whether warmer weather brings more of them out.
W: Exactly. And I checked with the caretaker yesterday. He isn't going to mow that patch until November.
M: You've already asked him? All right, you've convinced me. Keep your counts in a notebook and show it to me every Friday, so I can see how it's going.
W: Great, thanks so much. I'll bring the first page tomorrow, with the temperatures written in.

sets.title: Why worms come up in the rain
sets.transcript:
So, here's something you've all seen. After a heavy spring rain, you walk to school and the paths are covered in earthworms. Dozens of them, sometimes hundreds. Maybe you've stepped around them on the way here. Why are they there? If you ask most people, they'll tell you the worms came up so they wouldn't drown. The rain fills their tunnels with water, so they have to escape. It's a reasonable idea. I believed it myself for years. But today I want to show you why it doesn't fit the evidence, and what the other explanation is.

Let's start with how a worm breathes. A worm has no lungs. It takes in oxygen through its skin, and it can only do that while the skin is wet. In other words, water isn't the worm's enemy. It needs water to breathe. And rainwater soaking into the ground carries oxygen down with it. In fact, researchers have kept earthworms completely under water for several days, and many of them survived just fine.

Now, here's something our own class noticed. Last spring, after a storm, a group of students counted the worms on the path beside the car park. They found more than two hundred on a stretch about twenty metres long, and they counted them while it was still raining. But the lawn right next to the path wasn't flooded. The ground was soft, but there wasn't a single puddle on it. And most of the worms they counted weren't lying still. They were crawling along, some of them a long way from the grass.

So what's the other explanation? Think about how hard it is for a worm to get anywhere underground. It has to push or eat its way through the soil, a few centimetres at a time. That's slow, tiring work. On the surface, it can move much faster. The problem is that on a normal day, the surface is dangerous. The air dries out its skin, and sunlight harms it. A rainy day removes both problems. The ground is wet, and the sky is cloudy. So some scientists now think rain is simply a chance to travel, to reach a new patch of soil, and for some kinds of worms, to find a partner.

And that brings us back to the paths. Hard paths and roads dry out very quickly once the rain stops and the sun comes out. Grass and soil stay damp much longer, so a worm crossing a lawn is fairly safe. But a worm that has crawled out into the middle of a wide path usually can't get back to the soil in time.

So, next time someone tells you that worms come up to escape drowning, you can tell them that idea doesn't hold up. The worms aren't running from the rain. They're using it. And if you find one stranded on a path after the rain, you know what to do. Pick it up gently and put it back on the grass.
